title: Publication and the opening
short: First published 29 January 1845 in the New York Evening Mirror; also in the American Review (February 1845) as by 'Quarles'.
body: The poem was printed in the Evening Mirror on 29 January 1845, in advance of the American Review's February issue, where it appeared under the pseudonym '---- Quarles' (after Francis Quarles, author of the popular Emblems, 1635). It was an instant success and was much reprinted and parodied. Mabbott dates the composition to 1844. The fairy-tale opening 'Once upon a' sets a deliberately familiar, story-telling tone. Mabbott notes that it resembles the opening of an ode in the Anacreontea (no. 33), in which Love knocks at the poet's door at midnight, a parallel noticed by several scholars including Gilbert Highet.

title: Metre, stanza and internal rhyme
short: Trochaic octameter with dense internal rhyme; Poe took the stanza's model from Elizabeth Barrett's 'Lady Geraldine's Courtship'.
body: Each stanza has five long trochaic lines (eight feet, the alternate lines lacking the final syllable) and a short refrain line; Poe described the scheme in 'The Philosophy of Composition' and claimed originality for the stanza's combination rather than for its lines. The middle of each long line rhymes internally ('dreary' / 'weary', 'napping' / 'tapping'), and lines 2, 4, 5 and 6 share the '-ore' rhyme. Mabbott identifies Elizabeth Barrett's 'Lady Geraldine's Courtship' (1844) as the 'cardinal source' of the form; Poe dedicated The Raven and Other Poems (1845) to her. The prefatory note in the American Review commented on the poem's 'unique rhyming' and alliteration.

title: quaint ... forgotten lore
short: Old, odd books of obscure learning: the speaker is a scholar seeking distraction in study.
body: 'Quaint' here means curiously old-fashioned or ingeniously odd, and 'lore' is learning, especially traditional or esoteric knowledge. The speaker is a solitary student, as Poe said in 'The Philosophy of Composition' (which also gives his reason for the bust of Pallas: it suits the lover's scholarship). In stanza 2 we learn that he has sought in books 'surcease of sorrow'. Mabbott records that Poe asked Susan Talley whether 'many a' volume (rather than one) was proper, and defends it: a scholar turns from one book to another.

anchor: it was in the bleak December
title: the bleak December
short: Winter and dying embers set the mood; Mabbott hears an echo of Keats's 'In a drear-nighted December'.
body: The memory is fixed in December, at night, with each 'dying ember' casting its 'ghost' (the shadowy glow or shape of the coal) on the floor. Mabbott suggests an echo of Keats's lyric beginning 'In a drear-nighted December', available in American reprints of the Galignani edition, and of a December knocking in William Wirt's Old Bachelor (1814). The dying fire and its ghost quietly anticipate the poem's concern with loss and haunting.

sources.cite: T. O. Mabbott, ed., The Collected Works of Edgar Allan Poe, vol. I: Poems (Harvard UP, 1969), 'The Raven', pp. 350-374 (online at the Poe Society of Baltimore)
John Keats, 'Stanzas' ('In a drear-nighted December')

title: surcease
short: Cessation, end; he hoped his books would bring an end to grief. The word recalls Macbeth's 'his surcease'.
body: 'Surcease' means cessation or stopping (from Old French sursis, past participle of surseoir, 'to delay, suspend'). Already archaic in Poe's time, it is best known from Macbeth 1.7.4, 'catch, / With his surcease, success', where it means Duncan's death. Poe's phrase, alliterating on 's', names what the speaker seeks throughout the poem, an end to sorrow, which the bird will repeatedly deny, most directly in the nepenthe stanza.

title: Lenore
short: The dead beloved, probably imaginary; Poe had used the name in his earlier poem 'Lenore' (1843).
body: Lenore is the 'rare and radiant maiden' whose death the speaker mourns. Poe used the name in 'Lenore' (1843), and the type recurs in his tales ('Ligeia', 'Eleonora'). In 'The Philosophy of Composition' he argued that the death of a beautiful woman is 'the most poetical topic in the world', voiced by her bereaved lover. Mabbott thinks her almost surely imaginary, though some biographers see Poe's young wife Virginia, then ill with tuberculosis, as a prototype. The long 'o' and 'r' of 'Lenore' chime with the refrain 'Nevermore'.

title: Nameless here
short: No longer named or spoken to on earth: the angels call her Lenore, but in this world no one does.
body: Mabbott glosses 'Nameless here' as 'not called on by name or spoken to in this world'. The angels 'name' her in heaven; on earth her name has fallen silent, except when the speaker whispers it into the darkness in stanza 5. 'For evermore' anticipates the 'Nevermore' that will dominate the poem. The rhyme-word joins the '-ore' chain that runs through every stanza ('lore', 'door', 'floor', 'Lenore'), so that her name is woven into the poem's sound even while she is said to be nameless.

title: the purple curtain
short: Echoes, almost word for word, a line in Barrett's 'Lady Geraldine's Courtship'; purple suggests wealth and mourning.
body: The line 'the silken sad uncertain rustling of each purple curtain' closely echoes Elizabeth Barrett's 'With a rushing stir, uncertain, in the air, the purple curtain' in 'Lady Geraldine's Courtship' (1844). Mabbott records a report that Poe said the suggestion of his poem lay wholly in that line; the debt was noticed in 1845 by Thomas Dunn English. The sound of the line imitates rustling through its sibilants. Mabbott adds that purple may symbolise both wealth and mourning.

title: 'Sir ... or Madam'
short: The anxious politeness to an unseen visitor verges on comedy; Poe said he tested how near to the absurd he could come.
body: The speaker addresses the unseen knocker with exaggerated courtesy. Mabbott notes that a parrot is addressed as 'Sir, or Madam' in John Wilson's Noctes Ambrosianae (Blackwood's, 1829), with a talking raven on the following page. He also records Poe's remark that he wrote the poem 'to see how near to the absurd' he could come without crossing the line. The American Review introduction similarly mentioned 'ludicrous touches' amid the serious; the comedy heightens the eeriness.

sources.cite: T. O. Mabbott, ed., The Collected Works of Edgar Allan Poe, vol. I: Poems (Harvard UP, 1969), 'The Raven', pp. 350-374 (online at the Poe Society of Baltimore)

title: ''Tis the wind'
short: The speaker rationalises the tapping as wind; Mabbott compares Othello's 'It's the wind'.
body: Each early stanza ends with a reassuring dismissal, 'nothing more', which grows less convincing as it recurs. Mabbott compares Othello 4.3, where Desdemona hears a knock and Emilia answers 'It's the wind', and Poe's own 'Tell-Tale Heart', 'It is nothing but the wind in the chimney'. The refrain prepares for its own replacement by 'Nevermore' from stanza 8. Here the explanation is half true: when the shutter is opened, the wind is indeed there, but so is the Raven.

Shakespeare, Othello 4.3 (Folger Shakespeare)

title: flirt
short: A quick jerky movement; Johnson's Dictionary gives 'a quick elastic motion'.
body: 'Flirt' here is a sudden jerk or flick, the bird's abrupt motion of wings and tail, not flirtation. Mabbott cites a reviewer of 1850 who pointed to Johnson's Dictionary for the sense 'a quick, elastic motion'. Mabbott also records Poe's view that 'shutter' in the same line was too commonplace. The reviewer, who had once owned a raven, praised the bird's movements as true to life.

anchor: of the saintly days of yore
title: saintly days of yore
short: Ravens figure in scripture and saints' legends: Noah's raven, and the ravens that fed Elijah.
body: The bird is 'of the saintly days of yore' ('yore': long ago), an ironic halo for a black bird of ill omen. In Genesis 8:7 Noah sends out a raven from the ark; in 1 Kings 17:6 ravens bring bread and flesh to the prophet Elijah. Ravens also feed hermit saints in later legend. The phrase looks forward to the speaker's calling the bird 'Prophet!'. Mabbott adds that ravens were proverbially long-lived (Pliny), supporting the bird's 'ancient' character in stanza 8.

title: Pallas
short: Pallas Athena (Roman Minerva), goddess of wisdom; the bird of ill omen perches on the image of reason.
body: Pallas is an epithet of Athena, goddess of wisdom and patron of scholars. In 'The Philosophy of Composition' Poe said he chose the bust for its contrast with the black plumage, because it suited the lover's scholarship, and because 'Pallas' itself is sonorous. Busts of Minerva were popular ornaments; Mabbott records a story that one stood above a door in the Brennan farmhouse where Poe stayed in 1844. The image of the raven settled on wisdom's head is often read as grief or irrational dread mastering reason. Athena's own bird is the owl, and Mabbott notes Poe's reported first plan of an owl.

anchor: thy crest be shorn and shaven
title: shorn and shaven ... craven
short: 'Craven' means coward; cowardly knights were sometimes shaved. Mabbott sees a deliberate pun on 'knightly'.
body: The speaker teases the bird, whose head feathers look flattened, by saying that despite its 'shorn and shaven' crest it is 'sure no craven' (coward). Mabbott explains that a cowardly knight might have his head shaved as a mark of disgrace, and thinks the pun on 'knightly' and 'Nightly' (next line) deliberate, one of the poem's humorous touches. He also notes the legend in Don Quixote that King Arthur was turned into a raven.

title: Plutonian shore
short: Of Pluto, god of the underworld: the bird seems to come from the shore of the land of the dead.
body: Pluto (Greek Plouton) ruled the classical underworld, reached by crossing the Styx or Acheron. The 'Plutonian shore' is the bank of the river of the dead, and 'Night's' makes it the realm of darkness. Mabbott compares Horace, Odes 1.4.16-17, 'domus exilis Plutonia' ('the meagre house of Pluto'), which he says is the passage from which the Latin adjective is cited. The phrase recurs in stanza 17, when the speaker orders the bird back there.

title: The refrain 'Nevermore'
short: Poe said he chose the word for its long 'o' and 'r', the most sonorous vowel and most prolongable consonant.
body: In 'The Philosophy of Composition' Poe explained that he wanted a one-word refrain, that the long 'o' was 'the most sonorous vowel' and 'r' the most easily prolonged consonant, and that 'Nevermore' presented itself at once. He chose a non-reasoning creature to speak it so that the repetition would be natural, and a raven rather than a parrot for its ill-omened tone. The poem's design is that the same word acquires changing meanings as the speaker's questions grow more desperate. 'Quoth' is the archaic past tense of 'quethe', to say. Mabbott notes that 'nevermore' was common in English poetry, for instance in Shelley.

sources.cite: Edgar Allan Poe, 'The Philosophy of Composition', Graham's Magazine, April 1846

title: burden
short: A refrain or chorus, and also a load: the unhappy master's songs all carried the burden 'Never - nevermore'.
body: The speaker rationalises the word as the bird's 'only stock and store', learned from an 'unhappy master' pursued by Disaster until his songs 'one burden bore'. 'Burden' means the refrain of a song (from the French bourdon, a drone), and also a weight; both senses apply. 'Followed fast and followed faster' echoes, as Mabbott notes, Midsummer Night's Dream 3.2.416, 'I followed fast, but faster did he fly'. Mabbott also records that Poe removed a 'bad rhyme' from this eleventh stanza within a week of first publication.

title: velvet violet lining
short: Lenore will never again press the cushion; the lamp 'gloating' over it means shining upon it.
body: The cushion's lining, lit by the lamp, prompts the thought that Lenore will never sit there again. Mabbott notes that 'gloated' here has the rare sense 'reflected light from', though in Poe it usually carries something sinister; that Poe regarded 'lining' as a blunder but would not sacrifice the stanza; and that he had used 'velvet violet' before in a parody. Here the speaker himself, not the bird, pronounces 'nevermore' of Lenore, a turn in his own understanding.

sources.cite: T. O. Mabbott, ed., The Collected Works of Edgar Allan Poe, vol. I: Poems (Harvard UP, 1969), 'The Raven', pp. 350-374 (online at the Poe Society of Baltimore)

title: censer and Seraphim
short: Incense swung by angels: Seraphim are the six-winged angels of Isaiah 6; the 'tinkling' feet were much mocked.
body: A censer is a vessel for burning incense, swung in worship. The Seraphim are the angels seen by Isaiah about God's throne (Isaiah 6:2). The speaker imagines the air thickened with heavenly incense, a sign that God has sent him relief. The 'foot-falls' that 'tinkled on the tufted floor' were criticised in Poe's time; Mabbott reports that Thomas Dunn English asked whether the angels had bells on their toes, and that F. W. Thomas reported Poe had referred him to Isaiah 3:16, where the daughters of Zion make 'a tinkling with their feet'. Mabbott compares similar censers in 'Ligeia' and 'Eleonora'.

title: nepenthe
short: A drug of forgetfulness that Helen gives in the Odyssey; the speaker hopes to drink and forget Lenore.
body: In Odyssey 4.219-221 Helen puts into the wine a drug from Egypt, nepenthes (Greek ne-, 'not', and penthos, 'grief'), which banishes sorrow and anger. Mabbott also cites Spenser's Faerie Queene IV.iii.43 and Milton's Comus. 'Respite' is relief or pause. The speaker interprets the perfume as heaven sending him forgetfulness; the bird's 'Nevermore' denies it, making the bird a figure of unending memory. (The archive's text has a misprint, 'aad', for 'and' in the preceding line.)

title: 'Prophet!'
short: The speaker treats the bird as an oracle; ravens were prophetic birds in classical lore, sacred to Apollo.
body: From here the speaker asks the bird questions as if it could foretell the future. Mabbott hears an echo of Agamemnon's abuse of the seer Calchas in Pope's Iliad (1.106), 'Augur accurst! denouncing mischief still', and notes the ancient lore of ravens as prophetic birds sacred to Apollo, recorded by Pliny. Poe had complained in reviewing Dickens's Barnaby Rudge (1842) that Grip the raven's croakings were not made prophetic; here he does it himself. 'Tempter' suggests Satan; the bird may be 'bird or devil'.

title: balm in Gilead
short: From Jeremiah 8:22, 'Is there no balm in Gilead?': is there any healing or comfort for his grief?
body: Gilead, a region east of the Jordan, was famed for an aromatic healing resin (Genesis 37:25). Jeremiah's lament, 'Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there?' (Jeremiah 8:22), became proverbial for asking whether any cure exists for affliction. Mabbott notes that Poe's use is figurative, as elsewhere in his work. The question is the first of the two great questions the speaker puts, and the bird answers it with despair. The 'desert land enchanted' and the 'home by Horror haunted' (where Mabbott says the old pronunciation of 'haunted' means the rhyme was almost surely not imperfect for Poe) intensify the desolation.

title: Aidenn
short: Poe's exotic spelling of Eden, meaning Paradise: will he embrace Lenore in heaven?
body: Mabbott explains 'Aidenn' as Poe's unusual spelling of Eden (Arabic 'Adn), used also in 'The Conversation of Eiros and Charmion' and 'The Power of Words'. The second great question is whether the speaker's soul will meet Lenore in Paradise; 'Nevermore' answers that even the hope of reunion is denied. Mabbott compares the solemn adjuration 'by that God whom thou didst adore' in Cary's translation of Dante's Inferno 1.

title: beak in the heart
short: The first metaphor in the poem, Poe said: it signals that the bird should now be read as an emblem.
body: In 'The Philosophy of Composition' Poe identified 'from out my heart' as the poem's first metaphorical expression, designed, with the answer 'Nevermore', to make the reader seek a moral or meaning in all that has been narrated. The bird, which has been a literal raven, becomes an image of grief tearing at the speaker, like the eagle at Prometheus's liver. The speaker's furious command is met by the unchanging refrain.

sources.cite: Edgar Allan Poe, 'The Philosophy of Composition', Graham's Magazine, April 1846
T. O. Mabbott, ed., The Collected Works of Edgar Allan Poe, vol. I: Poems (Harvard UP, 1969), 'The Raven', pp. 350-374 (online at the Poe Society of Baltimore)

title: The emblematic ending
short: The bird sits still, for ever: Poe said the final stanza reveals it as 'Mournful and Never-ending Remembrance'.
body: The last stanza shifts to the present tense: the Raven 'still is sitting' on the bust, and the speaker's soul 'Shall be lifted - nevermore!'. Poe wrote that only here is the bird's emblematic meaning, 'Mournful and Never-ending Remembrance', permitted to be seen. Mabbott quotes C. Alphonso Smith that there is no trace of remorse in the ending, against critics who find guilt. John M. Daniel's 1849 introduction (perhaps reflecting Poe's talk) called the last stanza an image of settled despair added afterwards. Mabbott quotes Poe's letter to Eveleth explaining the lamp-light by a bracket candelabrum high above the door and bust.

sources.cite: Edgar Allan Poe, 'The Philosophy of Composition', Graham's Magazine, April 1846
T. O. Mabbott, ed., The Collected Works of Edgar Allan Poe, vol. I: Poems (Harvard UP, 1969), 'The Raven', pp. 350-374 (online at the Poe Society of Baltimore)

anchor: my soul from out that shadow
title: the shadow on the floor
short: The raven's shadow covers the floor and the speaker's soul lies in it; it 'shall be lifted - nevermore'.
body: The poem ends with the speaker's soul trapped in the shadow cast by the bird, an image of despair which completes the opening stanza's ember casting 'its ghost upon the floor'. Mabbott records that Poe explained to a correspondent he imagined a bracket candelabrum above the door. The final 'nevermore!' is spoken by the speaker of himself, and so differs from the bird's quoted refrain.
